comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C20-C26. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers strongly support the core behavioral finding that male-female interaction produces sleep deprivation without rebound. Peer reviewers describe this as 'very nicely' shown with 'strong' data, making it 'an important paper for that reason alone.'

Perfect agreement on claims C45-C47. Both evaluations support findings about pheromone exposure and sexual experience contributing to rebound suppression. These experiments appear to have been added in response to initial reviewer concerns, and both evaluations now find them convincing.

Perfect agreement on claims C3, C4, C59. Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support the central conclusion that sexual arousal modulates sleep homeostasis. Peer reviewers describe this as 'innovative' and 'the most in-depth investigation of how social interactions affect sleep to date.'

Disagreement on claims C63-C64. OpenEval finds the characterization of rebound suppression nature supported, while peer Reviewer #3 expresses uncertainty, asking whether the authors examined sleep architecture changes and arousal thresholds in detail.

Disagreement on claim C28 regarding R2 neuronal activity. OpenEval finds this cellular validation convincing, but peer Reviewer #3 questions whether pheromone exposure alone might reduce CaLexA activity signals, expressing uncertainty about the interpretation.

Disagreement on claim C34 (anosmic mutants). OpenEval finds the orco mutant data effectively excludes volatile olfactory signals, but peer reviewers express uncertainty about the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, noting altered time course and very small effects.

Disagreement on claim C43 (pheromone addition experiments). OpenEval supports the gain-of-function evidence, but peer reviewers express uncertainty, with Reviewer #3 stating 'The claim that sleep pressure after sleep deprivation can be counteracted by the mere presence of aphrodisiac pheromones is not fully supported by the data' and requesting additional direct experiments.

Strong disagreement on claim C44 (ppk neuronal activation). OpenEval finds artificial neuronal activation establishes sufficiency, but peer reviewers find this unsupported, citing missing controls (GAL4 and UAS lines alone) and concerns that temperature effects rather than neuronal manipulation may explain results.

Agreement on claims C29-C31 (memory mutants). OpenEval supports these findings, and peer reviewers implicitly accept them by not raising concerns and noting the authors used 'state-of-the art genetical tools' in an 'elegant set up.'

Partial overlap on claims C32-C33 (heterospecific females). OpenEval strongly supports the species-specificity control, and peer reviewers appear to accept these findings as part of the 'elegant set up' without raising specific concerns.

Disagreement on claim C37 (pheromone addition). OpenEval supports the gain-of-function evidence, but peer Reviewer #2 expresses major concerns about whether female CHCs induced a clear effect on sleep rebound, citing alternative explanations related to activity levels.

Strong disagreement on claims C41-C42 (ppk23 mutants). OpenEval finds the loss-of-function evidence strongly supportive, but peer reviewers find it unsupported. Reviewer #1 states 'There is also a problem with the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B' and notes the authors 'cut out the main effects which are seen later' by selecting the ZT0-3 window.

Agreement on claims C51-C52 (P1 neuron activation). Both OpenEval and peer reviewers support these findings. Peer reviewers note the authors 'elegantly show that sleep rebound is specifically affected by manipulating pheromonal sensory input, or arousal neurons themselves.'

Agreement on claim C55 (octopaminergic system). Both evaluations support the TβH mutant findings. OpenEval finds they support the arousal intensity hypothesis, and peer reviewers accept the revised manuscript without raising concerns about these experiments.

Agreement on claim C58 (bisexual mutants). Both evaluations support findings that arousal state rather than sex-specific features drives the effect. Peer reviewers' acceptance of the revised manuscript indicates support for these conclusions.
